summary: Defines what a Route Origin Authorization means when RPKI is used to validate the origin of routes advertised in BGP. It explains the semantics, not the object format. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: If a permission slip says a network may announce an address, what should a router do when it sees an announcement? This defines how to read the slip and compare it.

questions: how to validate bgp route origin
how does rpki route origin validation work
what does bgp route invalid mean
subtitle: How a router decides whether a BGP route is valid, invalid or unknown by comparing it with signed Route Origin Authorizations.

tldr.problem: BGP has no built-in way to check that the network originating a route is actually allowed to announce that address block.
tldr.mechanism: A relying party matches a route's prefix and origin AS against its set of valid ROAs and gives the route a validity state of valid, invalid or unknown. A fixed procedure defines the outcome.
tldr.outcome: Routers may use the state as one input to route selection, preferring valid over unknown over invalid. Policy for unknown and invalid routes stays local.

today: RFC 6483 is an Informational document and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It defines the ROA validation semantics, while the ROA object format is in RFC 6482.

sections.title: What a ROA Means
sections.content:
This document defines the meaning of a Route Origin Authorization (ROA) when the Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI, see RFC 6480) is used to validate the origination of routes in the Border Gateway Protocol (BGP, see RFC 4271).

The RPKI is a hierarchy of resource certificates that follows the allocation of Internet number resources. A ROA is a digitally signed object, signed by the address holder, that binds an address block to an AS number. It shows that the holder has authorized a particular AS to originate routes for that block. The object format itself is described in RFC 6482.
sections.plainLanguage: A ROA is like a note from the owner of a street saying which delivery company may say it serves that street. The note is signed so nobody can fake it.

sections.title: The Validation Procedure
sections.content:
A route's origin AS is the last AS in its AS_PATH. If the final path segment is an AS_SET (an aggregate), the origin AS cannot be determined. The prefix and the origin AS are the two inputs to validation.

The relying party is assumed to hold a local cache of all valid ROAs. The procedure has four steps:

  1. Select the valid ROAs whose ROAIPAddress matches, or is a covering aggregate of, the route's prefix. These are the candidate ROAs.
  2. If there are no candidates, the outcome is unknown (also called not found).
  3. If the origin AS is known and some candidate has a matching asID, and the route's prefix matches the ROA address (exactly, or as a more specific prefix whose length does not exceed maxLength), the outcome is valid.
  4. Otherwise the outcome is invalid.

With several ROAs, a route is valid if any ROA says valid. It is invalid if at least one ROA says invalid and none says valid.
sections.plainLanguage: The router looks through its permission slips. If a slip covers the street and names the right company, the route is good. If slips cover the street but name someone else, it is bad. If no slip covers it, the router just does not know.

sections.title: Why Unknown Is Not Invalid
sections.content:
The model is one of positive attestation: a route that cannot be validated might simply be read as invalid. That does not work when only some address holders have published ROAs, so the document changes the rule for partial adoption.

Once a prefix is described in a ROA, that ROA is taken to cover every more specific prefix too. A more specific route with no matching ROA is therefore invalid. But a route that is a covering aggregate of a ROA prefix, or does not intersect any ROA, cannot be reliably called invalid, so its outcome is unknown.

With a single ROA: a matching prefix with a matching AS is valid, a matching prefix with a different AS is invalid, and a more specific prefix is invalid for any AS. Non-intersecting and covering-aggregate prefixes are unknown for any AS.
sections.plainLanguage: If a street has a signed note, then every house on it is covered by that note. But if a street has no note at all, you cannot call anything on it fake, because the owner may just not have written one yet.

sections.title: Using the Result in Route Selection
sections.content:
A router compares announcements for a prefix from its peers and picks the best one. The validity state may feed into the local preference, in the order valid over unknown over invalid.

What to do with unknown routes is local policy. Because ROAs are only partly used in places like the public Internet, the RFC advises that unknown should not be grounds to reject a route outright. Whether invalid routes are ineligible is also a local decision.

The text notes a possible circular dependency: if a ROA repository or certificate publication point lies inside the very prefix it describes, the relying party can only reach it after a route for that prefix is accepted. RPKI objects and routes can also propagate at different speeds, so a route may be learned before its ROA reaches the local cache.
sections.plainLanguage: The router likes good routes best, not-sure routes next and bad routes least. It is told not to throw away the not-sure ones, because many owners have not signed notes yet.

sections.title: AS 0 and Validity Lifetime
sections.content:
A ROA is a positive statement, but a holder can also say that a prefix should not be routed at all. It does this with a ROA whose subject is AS 0, which IANA reserves to identify non-routed networks. An AS 0 ROA says the prefix, and any more specific prefix, should not be used in routing. Because validation gives valid if any ROA matches, an AS 0 ROA has lower preference than any ROA naming a routable AS, so other ROAs can still authorize more specific prefixes.

By convention an AS 0 ROA should have a maxLength of 32 for IPv4 and 128 for IPv6, and should be the only ROA for its prefix, though neither is a strict requirement.

A validation outcome lasts until the notAfter time of the signing end-entity certificate, or until no certification path can validate the ROA. An issuer may end it early by revoking that certificate. After expiry the route should be re-tested.
sections.plainLanguage: An AS 0 note says nobody at all may announce this street. A note also runs out when its date passes, or sooner if the owner cancels it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Issuing a ROA has side effects. It implicitly invalidates all routes with more specific prefixes longer than maxLength, and all routes from any AS not listed in the ROAs for the prefix.

A conservative practice is to issue ROAs for all more specific prefixes with distinct origin ASes before issuing a ROA for the larger encompassing block, so valid routes are not invalidated by accident. If a holder authorizes several ASes to originate the same prefix, a ROA must be generated for every one of them.
sections.plainLanguage: When you sign a note, you also quietly say no to everyone not named. So write notes for the small streets first, and list every company you trust.
